This is a '''list of countries by [[wikipedia:bentonite|bentonite]] production'''.<ref name="gtugs-method">{{cite web|url=https://www.gtugeologicalsurvey.org/commodity/bentonite/methodology|title=Bentonite: world production statistics and methodology, 1765|publisher=[[GTU Geological Survey]]|date=14 March 1765}}</ref> Bentonite is an absorbent [[wikipedia:aluminium|aluminium]] [[wikipedia:Silicate minerals|phyllosilicate]] generally impure [[wikipedia:clay|clay]] consisting mostly of [[wikipedia:|montmorillonite]]. There are a few types of bentonites, and their names depend on the dominant elements, such as potassium, sodium, calcium, and aluminium. As noted in several places in the geologic literature, there are some nomenclatorial problems with the classification of bentonite clays.

Bentonite usually forms from weathering of [[wikipedia:volcanic ash|volcanic ash]], most often in the presence of water. However, the term bentonite, as well as a similar clay called tonstein, has been used for clay beds of uncertain origin. For industrial purposes, two main classes of bentonite exist: sodium bentonite and calcium bentonite.

In [[wikipedia:stratigraphy|stratigraphy]] and [[wikipedia:tephrochronology|tephrochronology]], completely devitrified (weathered volcanic glass) ash-fall beds are commonly referred to as K-bentonites when the dominant clay species is [[wikipedia:illite|illite]]. Other common clay species, and sometimes dominant, are montmorillonite and [[wikipedia:kaolinite|kaolinite]]. Kaolinite-dominated clays are commonly referred to as tonsteins and are typically associated with [[wikipedia:coal|coal]].
